question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Necassery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Necassery" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "necessary", an adjective meaning needed; required; essential. (आवश्यक)

◦ Correct: It is necessary to carry your admit card to the examination hall.

• Spelling key: NE + CES + SA + RY — remember the mnemonic "one C, two S's" (like a shirt has one Collar and two Sleeves).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "Humorous" (funny, amusing) is correctly spelt — note that "humour" drops the 'u' when it becomes "humorous".

• "Apparent" (clearly visible or obvious) is correctly spelt — one 'p' + double 'r'.

• "Definite" (clearly stated, certain) is correctly spelt — note "definite", never "definate".

NOTE

• Frequently misspelt SSC words: necessary, occasion, accommodation, embarrass, harass, committee, maintenance, privilege, separate, occurrence.

• Related forms: necessary (adjective), necessity (noun), necessarily (adverb), necessitate (verb).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.

A small shop that sells fashionable clothes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Boutique.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "boutique" is a small shop selling fashionable clothes or accessories. The word comes from French and exactly matches the given definition. (बुटीक — फ़ैशनेबल कपड़ों की छोटी दुकान)

◦ Example: She bought her wedding outfit from a designer boutique in Delhi.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Store" is a general word for any shop; it does not carry the sense of "small" or "fashionable".

• Option 3 "Tailoring" is the work/business of making clothes, not a shop that sells them.

• Option 4 "Couture" means the design and making of high-quality fashionable clothes (as in "haute couture"); it is the craft, not the shop.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: Emporium (a large retail store), Kiosk (a small open-fronted stall), Bazaar (a market), Boutique (a small fashion shop), Arcade (a covered passage with shops).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

The blue is a beautiful colour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The blue.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Names of colours used as common nouns in a general sense do not take the definite article "the". Hence "The blue" is wrong; it should simply be "Blue".

◦ Correct: Blue is a beautiful colour.

• The article "the" is used only when the noun is particular/specific (e.g., "the blue of her eyes", "the blue in this painting").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• "is" correctly agrees with the singular subject.

• "a" is the right indefinite article before the consonant sound /b/ in "beautiful".

• "beautiful colour" is a correct adjective + noun combination.

NOTE

• "The" is omitted before: names of colours, languages (Hindi, English), games (cricket), meals (lunch), subjects (Physics), abstract nouns used generally (Honesty is the best policy) and proper nouns of most countries, cities and persons.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The Nile is the ________ river of the world.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. longest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "of the world" indicates a comparison with all rivers, i.e. the superlative degree. With the definite article "the" before the blank, the superlative "longest" is required.

◦ Correct: The Nile is the longest river of the world.

• Degrees of comparison: long (positive) – longer (comparative, used with "than") – (the) longest (superlative, used with "the" / "of all" / "in the world").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "long" (positive degree) cannot follow "the" in this comparative sense.

• Option 2 "longer" is comparative and needs "than" (e.g., The Nile is longer than the Amazon).

• Option 3 "more longer" is a double comparative — "more" can never be combined with the "-er" ending.

NOTE

• Superlative signals: the, of all, in the world, ever, among all. Comparative signal: than.

• Static fact: the Nile is generally regarded as the longest river in the world (about 6,650 km).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

Tuntun and her friends dance beautiful.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. beautiful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word that follows the verb "dance" must describe how the action is performed, so an adverb is needed, not an adjective. "Beautiful" is an adjective; the correct adverb is "beautifully".

◦ Correct: Tuntun and her friends dance beautifully.

• Rule: adjectives modify nouns/pronouns, while adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• "Tuntun" and "and her friends" together form a plural subject, so the plural verb "dance" (Option 1) is correct.

• There is no error in "and her friends" — the possessive "her" correctly refers to Tuntun.

NOTE

• Adjective → adverb conversions: beautiful → beautifully, careful → carefully, quick → quickly, happy → happily, true → truly.

• Watch out: verbs of sensation/state (look, seem, feel, taste, smell, sound, become) take an adjective, not an adverb — "She looks beautiful" is correct, but "She dances beautifully".

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

It’s risky to invest all your savings in one company; it’s like _______________.
option_2: putting all your eggs in one basket
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. putting all your eggs in one basket.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to put all your eggs in one basket" means to risk everything on a single venture / to depend entirely on one plan or one source. This exactly matches "investing all your savings in one company". (सारा दांव एक ही जगह लगाना)

◦ Example: Do not put all your eggs in one basket — diversify your investments.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "going down in flames" means to fail spectacularly/completely — it describes the failure, not the risky act of concentrating everything in one place.

• Option 3 "biting the bullet" means to endure a painful situation bravely.

• Option 4 "breaking a leg" is used to wish someone good luck, especially before a performance.

NOTE

• Related money/risk idioms: "hedge your bets" (reduce risk by backing more than one option), "a safe bet" (something certain), "take a punt" (take a chance), "diversify" (the literal advice behind this idiom).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined group of words.

Sometimes we have to accept replacing something with something else, if we want to move forward.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. change.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Change" means the act of replacing one thing with another; making or becoming different. This is precisely what "replacing something with something else" describes. (परिवर्तन / बदलाव)

◦ Correct: Sometimes we have to accept change, if we want to move forward.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Evaluation" means judging or assessing the value/quality of something — no replacement is involved.

• Option 3 "Invasion" means entering a place by force, especially with an army.

• Option 4 "Invention" means creating something entirely new that did not exist before, not swapping one thing for another.

NOTE

• Useful related words: substitution (putting one in place of another), exchange (giving one and receiving another), transformation (a complete change of form), alteration (a small change), modification (a partial change).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.

Dishevelled
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Tidy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Dishevelled" means untidy, messy, ruffled or disordered — especially of hair, clothes or appearance. Its antonym is "tidy", meaning neat and well arranged. (अस्त-व्यस्त का विलोम — व्यवस्थित)

◦ Example: After the long journey he looked dishevelled, but a bath and fresh clothes made him tidy again.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Assertive" (confident and forceful in stating one's views) is unrelated.

• Option 3 "Tainted" (contaminated or spoilt) is closer to a negative quality but does not oppose "untidy".

• Option 4 "Rigid" (stiff, inflexible) is unrelated to appearance.

NOTE

• Synonyms of dishevelled: unkempt, messy, rumpled, bedraggled, tousled, scruffy.

• Antonyms of dishevelled: tidy, neat, well-groomed, immaculate, orderly, spruce.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I ___________ to many countries to find the source of true happiness.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. travelled.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The only correctly spelt word among the options is "travelled" — the past tense/past participle of the verb "travel" (to go from one place to another). (यात्रा की)

◦ Correct: I travelled to many countries to find the source of true happiness.

• Spelling key: TRA + VEL + LED. In British English the final 'l' is doubled before "-ed" (travel → travelled); in American English it is not (traveled).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• The other options are all misspellings: "triveled", "travalled" and "travelld" — the correct base word is travel, not "trivel" or "traval".

NOTE

• Similar British doubling: travel → travelled/travelling, cancel → cancelled/cancelling, label → labelled, marvel → marvelled, quarrel → quarrelled.

• Related forms: travel (verb/noun), traveller (noun), travelogue (an account of one's travels).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Jugglary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Jugglary" is misspelt. The correct spelling is "jugglery", meaning the skill or act of juggling; trickery or deception. (जादूगरी / धोखाधड़ी)

◦ Correct: The accountant's jugglery with figures fooled the auditors for years.

• Spelling key: JUG + GLE + RY — it keeps the "-ery" ending, like "bakery", "robbery" and "trickery".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• "Abhorrent" (causing disgust or hatred) is correctly spelt.

• "Gesture" (a movement of the hand or head to express an idea) is correctly spelt.

• "Magnificence" (impressive beauty or splendour) is correctly spelt — note the "-ence" ending.

NOTE

• Words ending in -ery: jugglery, bakery, robbery, machinery, stationery (writing material), bravery, imagery.

• Do not confuse stationery (paper, pens) with stationary (not moving).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom in the following sentence.

Irrespective of the chaos in the classroom, our class teacher stays cool as a cucumber.
option_3: Scolds all the students in the classroom
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Stays calm and composed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "(as) cool as a cucumber" means extremely calm, relaxed and composed, especially in a difficult or stressful situation. (बिलकुल शांत और संयत रहना)

◦ Example: Even during the fire drill, the manager remained as cool as a cucumber.

• In the sentence, despite "the chaos in the classroom", the teacher does not lose her temper — she stays perfectly composed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "Behaves like a vegetable" is a literal, word-for-word misreading of the idiom — idioms are never interpreted literally.

• Option 3 "Scolds all the students in the classroom" is the opposite of staying calm.

• Option 4 "Develops a fever" has no connection with the idiom.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of calmness: "keep your cool", "keep a level head", "take it in one's stride", "not turn a hair", "as calm as a millpond".

• Opposite idioms: "fly off the handle", "lose one's cool", "hit the roof", "blow a fuse".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Hazard
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Accident.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Hazard" (noun) means a danger or risk; a source of possible harm; a mishap. Among the given choices, "accident" is the closest in sense, as both refer to an unwanted, harmful event or the risk of one. (ख़तरा / दुर्घटना)

◦ Example: Driving in dense fog is a serious hazard — many an accident happens on such nights.

• As a verb, "hazard" also means to venture or risk (e.g., "May I hazard a guess?").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "Marvel" means a wonderful or astonishing thing — a positive sense.

• Option 2 "Miracle" means an extraordinary event attributed to a supernatural cause — also positive.

• Option 3 "Ardent" is an adjective meaning passionate/enthusiastic, so it cannot be a synonym of a noun like hazard.

NOTE

• Synonyms of hazard: danger, risk, peril, jeopardy, threat, menace, accident.

• Antonyms of hazard: safety, security, protection, certainty.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

He is a smug and very ______ person who thinks only about himself.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. egoistic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Egoistic" means self-centred; concerned only with oneself and one's own interests. The clue phrases "smug" (self-satisfied) and "thinks only about himself" make this the perfect fit. (आत्मकेंद्रित / अहंकारी)

◦ Correct: He is a smug and very egoistic person who thinks only about himself.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "arsonist" is a noun meaning a person who deliberately sets fire to property; it cannot follow "very".

• Option 2 "diffident" means shy and lacking self-confidence — the opposite of smug.

• Option 4 "humble" means modest, not proud — it contradicts "thinks only about himself".

NOTE

• Synonyms of egoistic: egotistical, self-centred, narcissistic, conceited, vain, self-absorbed.

• Antonyms: humble, modest, selfless, altruistic, unassuming.

• Note the difference: egoism (acting in one's own self-interest) vs egotism (excessively talking about oneself).

question:
Select the word segment which substitutes the bracketed word correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully.

I (am here) since 1981.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. have been here.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "since" followed by a point of time (1981) with an action continuing up to the present requires the present perfect (or present perfect continuous) tense, not the simple present.

◦ Correct: I have been here since 1981.

• The subject "I" takes the auxiliary "have", not "has".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "had been here" is past perfect — it would need a second, later past action for reference.

• Option 3 "was here" is simple past and cannot be used with "since" in this sense.

• Option 4 "has been here" is wrong because "has" is used with third-person singular subjects (he/she/it), not with "I".

NOTE

• Rule: since + point of time (since 1981, since Monday, since morning); for + period of time (for 40 years, for two hours).

• Structure: Subject + has/have + been + ... + since/for ... (I have been here since 1981 / for four decades).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.

You shall repented tomorrow for your misdeeds.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. shall repented.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A modal auxiliary such as "shall/will/can/may/must" is always followed by the base form (V1) of the verb, never the past form (V2). Hence "shall repented" is wrong; it must be "shall repent".

◦ Correct: You shall repent tomorrow for your misdeeds.

• The adverb "tomorrow" also confirms a future action, which suits "shall repent".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "You" is a correct subject and "for your misdeeds" is a correct prepositional phrase.

• "tomorrow" is a correct adverb of time for the future tense.

NOTE

• Modal + V1: can go, may come, must work, should study, will write, shall repent.

• Traditional usage: "shall" with I/We for simple future, and with You/He/They it expresses command, threat, promise or determination — as in this sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

She think Alex is abandoning her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. thinks.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "She" is third person singular, so in the simple present tense the verb must take "-s": "thinks".

◦ Correct: She thinks Alex is abandoning her.

• The subordinate clause "Alex is abandoning her" is in the present continuous, so the main verb should also stay in the present for correct sequence of tenses.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "was thinking" (past continuous) and Option 2 "thought" (simple past) clash with the present-tense clause "is abandoning".

• Option 4 "was to think" is not a valid structure here.

• "Think" is a stative verb of mental state and is normally not used in the continuous form to express an opinion.

NOTE

• Subject–verb agreement: He/She/It + verb + s/es (she thinks, he goes, it works); I/We/You/They + base verb (they think).

• Sequence of tenses: a present-tense main clause is normally followed by a present-tense subordinate clause.

question:
Select the most appropriate segment that can substitute the bracketed word in the following sentence.

The bridge that (connecting) the two valleys across the Brahmaputra river has recently been constructed in Arunachal Pradesh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. connects.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The relative pronoun "that" introduces a relative clause which needs a finite verb. "Connecting" is a participle and cannot serve as the verb of that clause.

• The bridge's function of joining the two valleys is a permanent, general fact, so the simple present "connects" is used. The antecedent "The bridge" is singular, so the verb takes "-s".

◦ Correct: The bridge that connects the two valleys across the Brahmaputra river has recently been constructed in Arunachal Pradesh.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "will be connecting" and Option 3 "will be connected" wrongly place the action in the future, although the bridge "has recently been constructed" (already complete).

• Option 2 "had connected" (past perfect) would need an earlier past reference, which is absent.

NOTE

• Use the simple present for permanent truths, general facts and habitual actions: "The Ganga flows through Varanasi", "This road leads to the station".

• Static fact: the Bhupen Hazarika Setu (Dhola–Sadiya bridge) over the Lohit, a Brahmaputra tributary, links Assam and Arunachal Pradesh and is India's longest river bridge (9.15 km).

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.

Naina has six children, and I always ________ with their names.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. get mixed up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal idiom "get mixed up (with/about something)" means to become confused; to muddle one thing with another. With six children's names, confusing one for another is exactly the sense required. (गड़बड़ा जाना / भ्रमित हो जाना)

◦ Correct: Naina has six children, and I always get mixed up with their names.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "get rid of" means to remove or dispose of something unwanted — it does not fit "with their names".

• Option 3 "get away clean" means to escape without being caught or punished.

• Option 4 "get cold feet" means to lose one's nerve at the last moment.

NOTE

• More "get" idioms: "get the hang of" (learn how to do), "get on someone's nerves" (irritate), "get out of hand" (become uncontrollable), "get the better of" (defeat), "get a word in edgeways" (manage to speak).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

When it comes to planning her wedding, Maria wants ________________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. the whole nine yards.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "the whole nine yards" means everything possible; the full extent; all of it. For a wedding, it suggests Maria wants every arrangement done completely and lavishly. (सब कुछ, पूरा का पूरा)

◦ Correct: When it comes to planning her wedding, Maria wants the whole nine yards.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "down for the count" (from boxing) means defeated or unconscious/asleep.

• Option 2 "a black sheep" refers to a disgraceful member of a family or group.

• Option 3 "the whole fifteen miles" is not an idiom — it is a distractor built by altering the real idiom's numbers.

NOTE

• Similar idioms meaning "everything": "the whole shebang", "the works", "lock, stock and barrel", "the whole kit and caboodle", "hook, line and sinker".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

I know that I can count on my best friend to be by my side through ____ and thin.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. thick.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The fixed idiom is "through thick and thin", which means through both good and bad times; in all circumstances, no matter what happens. (हर परिस्थिति में साथ निभाना)

◦ Correct: I know that I can count on my best friend to be by my side through thick and thin.

• Idioms are fixed expressions — no word in them may be replaced, even by a synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• "through tough and thin", "through heavy and thin" and "through fat and thin" are not English idioms; they are invented distractors.

NOTE

• Other alliterative/paired idioms: "by hook or by crook", "part and parcel", "null and void", "safe and sound", "ups and downs", "give and take".

• Related friendship idioms: "a friend in need is a friend indeed", "stand by someone", "through the thick of it".

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I do not know how the party ended. I do not want to know. I went (1)___ upstairs, and undressed and (2)___ into bed, and lay there in the burning dark while the last guest gurgled in the hall below about the wonderful evening she had spent. I lay there (3)___ the front door shut after her, and Lavinia’s steps came up the stairs and passed the door to the guest room beyond. And then after a couple of centuries (4)___, the clock struck three and I (5)___ to sleep.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. straight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Go straight upstairs" means to go directly upstairs, without stopping or doing anything else on the way. The narrator, disgusted with the party, went directly to bed — hence "I went straight upstairs".

◦ Correct: I went straight upstairs, and undressed and crawled into bed ...

• Here "straight" is used as an adverb meaning "directly / immediately".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "over upstairs" is not a valid collocation.

• Option 2 "through upstairs" is grammatically wrong — "through" needs an object you pass inside of.

• Option 3 "around upstairs" would suggest wandering aimlessly, which contradicts the narrator's hurry to escape the party.

NOTE

• Useful collocations with "straight": go straight home, come straight to the point, look someone straight in the eye, tell it straight, straight away (immediately).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I do not know how the party ended. I do not want to know. I went (1)___ upstairs, and undressed and (2)___ into bed, and lay there in the burning dark while the last guest gurgled in the hall below about the wonderful evening she had spent. I lay there (3)___ the front door shut after her, and Lavinia’s steps came up the stairs and passed the door to the guest room beyond. And then after a couple of centuries (4)___, the clock struck three and I (5)___ to sleep.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. crawled.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Crawl into bed" is a common English collocation meaning to get into bed slowly and wearily, usually when one is exhausted or miserable. The narrator is drained after the party, so "undressed and crawled into bed" is the natural choice.

◦ Correct: ... I went straight upstairs, and undressed and crawled into bed ...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "gnawed" means to bite or chew persistently — it does not go with "into bed".

• Option 2 "lurched" means to make a sudden, unsteady movement; it suggests staggering, not settling down to sleep.

• Option 3 "peeped" means to look quickly and secretly — one cannot "peep into bed" in this sense.

NOTE

• Collocations with bed: crawl into bed, tumble into bed, slip into bed, get out of bed, make the bed, hit the sack/hay (go to bed).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I do not know how the party ended. I do not want to know. I went (1)___ upstairs, and undressed and (2)___ into bed, and lay there in the burning dark while the last guest gurgled in the hall below about the wonderful evening she had spent. I lay there (3)___ the front door shut after her, and Lavinia’s steps came up the stairs and passed the door to the guest room beyond. And then after a couple of centuries (4)___, the clock struck three and I (5)___ to sleep.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. while.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank joins two clauses — "I lay there" and "the front door shut after her, and Lavinia's steps came up the stairs ...". A subordinating conjunction of time is needed to show that the two actions happened at the same time. "While" (= during the time that) does exactly this.

◦ Correct: I lay there while the front door shut after her, and Lavinia's steps came up the stairs ...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "still" is an adverb and cannot join two clauses in this position.

• Option 2 "toward" is a preposition of direction and must be followed by a noun of place.

• Option 4 "down" is a preposition/adverb of direction and gives no time link.

NOTE

• Conjunctions of time: while, when, as, before, after, until, till, since, as soon as, no sooner ... than.

• "While" is used for actions in progress at the same time; "when" is used for a point of time.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I do not know how the party ended. I do not want to know. I went (1)___ upstairs, and undressed and (2)___ into bed, and lay there in the burning dark while the last guest gurgled in the hall below about the wonderful evening she had spent. I lay there (3)___ the front door shut after her, and Lavinia’s steps came up the stairs and passed the door to the guest room beyond. And then after a couple of centuries (4)___, the clock struck three and I (5)___ to sleep.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. elapsed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Elapse" is used specifically for time passing by. The subject here is "a couple of centuries" (a hyperbole for a very long stretch of time), so "after a couple of centuries elapsed" is the correct expression. (समय बीत जाना)

◦ Correct: And then after a couple of centuries elapsed, the clock struck three ...

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 "crossed" needs an object (cross a road/river) and is not used intransitively for time.

• Option 2 "eroded" means worn away gradually (used of soil, rock, confidence), not of time passing.

• Option 4 "persisted" means continued stubbornly, which contradicts "after ... the clock struck three".

NOTE

• Words for time passing: elapse, pass, go by, slip away, wear on, tick by.

• Note the hyperbole in "a couple of centuries" — the narrator only means that the wait felt endless.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I do not know how the party ended. I do not want to know. I went (1)___ upstairs, and undressed and (2)___ into bed, and lay there in the burning dark while the last guest gurgled in the hall below about the wonderful evening she had spent. I lay there (3)___ the front door shut after her, and Lavinia’s steps came up the stairs and passed the door to the guest room beyond. And then after a couple of centuries (4)___, the clock struck three and I (5)___ to sleep.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. dozed off.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "doze off" means to fall asleep, especially unintentionally or lightly. The clause ends with "to sleep", and the whole passage describes the narrator finally falling asleep at three o'clock.

◦ Correct: ... the clock struck three and I dozed off to sleep.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 "called off" means to cancel (call off a match/strike).

• Option 3 "took off" means to leave the ground (aircraft) / to remove (clothes) / to leave suddenly.

• Option 4 "put off" means to postpone or to discourage/repel.

NOTE

• Sleep-related expressions: doze off, nod off, drift off, drop off, fall asleep, hit the sack, catch forty winks.

• All four options use the particle "off" — always read the whole phrasal verb and test it against the context.
